case_study_insert.main_stem: Solaris Grid Energy (SGE) is a public limited company in the renewable energy sector, providing grid-scale battery storage and solar farm maintenance, with a workforce of 75. Founded in 2010 by Amina Bello, SGE operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership so safety rules are enforced on high-voltage sites. SGE plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new grid-battery testing facility and recycling plant, financed by a $900,000 ten-year bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $900,000 a year, a variable cost of $40.00 a unit and a selling price of $65.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. A safety-related skills gap and rising equipment defect rates are delaying maintenance contracts and raising costs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q1 2025: SGE completed 3,800 maintenance units with an equipment defect rate of 2.6%, up from 1.4% last year. Safety incidents rose from 7 to 16 a quarter and waste from replaced cells reached 4.8% of materials. A survey of 400 energy firms found that 77% require accredited battery technicians and 64% would switch supplier over poor safety records. Records show 18 of 75 technicians lack high-voltage accreditation; on-the-job training is given on site and off-the-job courses at the energy institute cost $1,250 per technician.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Solaris Grid Energy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (March 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.50%, increasing interest on SGE's $900,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $14.20 to $15.04 an hour, raising technician and site wage costs. (3) Lithium and solar-component input costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, while energy inflation is 8.4% and grid-storage demand grew 6.7%.

questions.question_text: SGE raised $600,000 through a share issue. Explain two advantages for SGE of funding part of its $1,500,000 facility this way rather than with more bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share issue proceeds never have to be repaid and carry no interest, which protects SGE's cash flow while it services the $900,000 ten-year bank loan and fixed costs of $900,000 a year. The $600,000 can therefore be directed into the grid-battery testing facility and into training the 18 technicians lacking accreditation, instead of being spent on interest. With a $25.00 contribution per unit on 60,000 units, preserving cash is vital while rising equipment defect rates delay contracts.

Point 2: Equity strengthens the balance sheet and reduces financial risk at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.50%. As a public limited company, SGE can broaden its shareholder base, avoiding the covenants and security a larger loan would demand, so it is better able to withstand safety incidents that have risen from 7 to 16 a quarter. There is no obligation to pay dividends unless profits allow, unlike loan interest, so the $600,000 supports growth without a fixed commitment. The cost is dilution of ownership, but for a capital-intensive energy business this is a sound way to fund expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over further borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SGE's expansion, financing and safety needs.

questions.question_text: SGE is promoting its new battery recycling plant. Consider trade journal advertising, sponsoring an energy conference, or social media marketing. Which should SGE choose to win grid contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journal advertising: Adverts in energy and utilities journals reach the technical buyers who commission grid-scale storage and maintenance, at a controlled cost for a firm funding a $1,500,000 plant. Detailed messages about recycling, accreditation and the falling 2.6% defect rate can be included, appealing to the 77% of 400 surveyed firms that require accredited technicians. Drawbacks are long lead times and narrow reach, so awareness may build slowly.

Sponsoring an energy conference: This gives SGE face-to-face access to senior engineers and procurement teams, with demonstrations and credibility in a specialist market, which matters when 64% of firms would switch supplier over safety records. It is expensive relative to the $900,000 loan, however, and its impact is limited to one event, so the message may not reach the wider market that could support 6.7% demand growth.

Social media marketing: Targeted campaigns can broadcast the recycling story and safety record cheaply to a broad audience with measurable engagement and rapid updates. Conversion to large grid contracts is slow and uncertain, and constant content is needed, but cost per contact is low.

Recommendation: SGE should choose trade journal advertising as its main channel, supported by social media. Journals reach the energy firms that decide grid contracts and can carry the accreditation message that 77% of buyers require, at a cost that fits alongside the $900,000 loan. Conference sponsorship is rejected as expensive and short-lived when safety incidents are already a concern; social media alone is rejected because it rarely wins large technical tenders, so it should complement rather than replace the trade campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal reference to SGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to SGE and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in SGE's context with a clear recommendation explaining why the conference and social-media-only options are rejected.

questions.question_text: SGE's safety incidents and 2.6% equipment defect rate are a concern. Explain two benefits for SGE of its autocratic leadership on high-voltage sites.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows founder Amina Bello to impose clear, consistent safety rules across a hierarchical structure, which is vital on high-voltage sites. Safety incidents have risen from 7 to 16 a quarter, so a single decisive instruction on lock-out procedures can be enforced immediately, reducing risk and helping cut the 2.6% equipment defect rate. This protects the 3,800 maintenance units completed each quarter and the contracts of the 64% of firms that would switch supplier over poor safety records.

Point 2: Centralised decisions speed up responses to faults and enforce the training message. When 18 of 75 technicians lack high-voltage accreditation, management can direct them onto the $1,250 per-technician courses without delay and verify standards uniformly, which supports the 77% of buyers who require accredited technicians. Clear direction also helps limit the 4.8% materials waste from replaced cells by standardising handling. This style suits a safety-critical operation, though SGE must watch that strict control does not hide reporting of incidents.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SGE's safety, defects and accreditation.

questions.question_text: SGE must train the 18 technicians lacking high-voltage accreditation. Consider on-the-job training on site or off-the-job courses at the energy institute. Which should SGE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on SGE's own sites is directly relevant to its high-voltage equipment and safety rules, costs no fees, and keeps technicians productive while they learn, protecting the 3,800 maintenance units completed each quarter. Experienced staff can demonstrate the exact checks that keep the 2.6% defect rate and 4.8% waste in hand. Weaknesses are that trainers are working technicians whose own duties suffer, bad habits may spread, and there is no independent certificate, which matters because 77% of buyers require accredited staff.

Off-the-job courses: The energy institute charges $1,250 per technician, so accrediting the 18 lacking staff would cost $22,500 (18 × $1,250), small beside the $1,500,000 facility. Courses give structured, up-to-date content and a recognised certificate that directly meets the 77% requirement and the 64% of firms concerned about safety records. However, technicians are away from sites, potentially slowing maintenance, and generic content may not match SGE's equipment exactly.

Decision: SGE should choose off-the-job courses for the 18 technicians, followed by on-site coaching. The recognised high-voltage certificate is essential when safety incidents have doubled to 16 and 77% of buyers demand accreditation, and $22,500 is affordable; on-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot award the qualification those clients require and may pass on unsafe local habits. The qualification also supports the 64% of firms concerned about safety records and helps retain technicians during a skills shortage, while the $22,500 cost is small beside the $1,500,000 facility. To limit disruption to the 3,800 maintenance units, SGE should stagger the 18 places and follow each course with on-site coaching on its own high-voltage equipment, so the certificate translates into safer practice and a lower 2.6% defect rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods with reference to SGE's costs and safety requirements.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in SGE's context with a justified decision covering safety, accreditation, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SGE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $900,000 ÷ ($65.00 − $40.00) = $900,000 ÷ $25.00 = 36,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 36,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $65.00 − $40.00 = $25.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $25.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SGE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 36,000-unit break-even output with 60,000 units actually delivered gives a margin of safety of 24,000 units, showing a useful buffer while safety incidents and the skills gap delay contracts.
2. Contribution of $25.00 a unit lets managers test price changes: a hypothetical $2.00 discount would cut contribution to $23.00 and raise break-even to $900,000 ÷ $23.00 = 39,130.43 units, indicating the volume needed to justify a competitive tender.
3. With fixed costs of $900,000, managers can set the maintenance-volume target needed to service the $900,000 loan and assess it against the 3,800 units completed each quarter before adding capacity.
4. Unit cost of $55.00 ($900,000 ÷ 60,000 units = $15.00 fixed cost per unit, plus $40.00 variable cost) can be tracked against the 13.2% lithium and solar-component inflation, while labour productivity of 60,000 units ÷ 75 staff = 800 units per worker helps judge the effect of the skills gap and 2.6% defect rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 36,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $25.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 24,000 units vs 60,000 output; discount modelling vs $900,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume target; and unit-cost benchmarking at $55.00 with productivity of 800 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SGE's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SGE's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Revenue of $12,000,000 in 2024 less cost of sales of $7,200,000 gives gross profit of $4,800,000; revenue of $13,500,000 in 2025 less $7,425,000 gives $6,075,000. Gross profit divided by revenue yields 40.0% and 45.0%. Operating profit of $1,800,000 in 2024 and $2,700,000 in 2025, each divided by revenue, yields 15.0% and 20.0%. Operating profit divided by capital employed of $10,000,000 and $12,000,000 yields 18.0% and 22.5%.

Evaluation: The improvement is strong and consistent. The first margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, showing SGE kept more of each revenue dollar after direct costs even as lithium and component prices climbed 13.2%, which is consistent with tighter control of the 60,000 units delivered. The overall margin improved from 15.0% to 20.0%, so overheads were absorbed much better as revenue grew by $1,500,000. The return on capital increased from 18.0% to 22.5%; although capital employed rose to $12,000,000 to fund the new testing facility, operating profit grew by 50%, so the extra investment is already productive. Interest payable fell from $300,000 to $280,000, easing the pressure of the $900,000 loan and rising base rates.

Conclusion: SGE's profitability has improved. All three ratios rose together, backed by higher revenue and gross profit and lower interest costs, so the gain is broad-based. The key caution is that the 13.2% input inflation and 5.9% wage rise could erode the 45.0% margin if the skills gap persists, so management should accelerate the 18 accreditation places and monitor materials waste of 4.8%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Correctly calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years with detailed evaluation of margins, capital efficiency and financing and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SGE of requiring high-voltage accreditation for its technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Requiring accreditation directly tackles the safety-related skills gap and answers the 77% of 400 surveyed energy firms that require accredited battery technicians. It also addresses the 64% that would switch supplier over poor safety records, supporting SGE's tendering position as it opens the $1,500,000 testing facility and helping protect the $25.00 contribution per unit against 13.2% component inflation.

Disadvantage: Accreditation costs time and money. The insert states off-the-job courses cost $1,250 per technician and that 18 of 75 staff are not accredited, so full coverage needs a real budget and time away from the 3,800 maintenance units completed each quarter, which may slow contracts further while safety incidents are already 16. The insert gives no breakdown of the $40.00 variable cost, so the payback cannot be quantified, and stricter requirements could make it harder to recruit technicians during a skills shortage. Unaccredited rivals could also undercut SGE's prices and win the 23% (100% − 77%) of surveyed firms that do not require certification, so the business must show that accreditation improves safety and reliability, not just cost. With 16 safety incidents already recorded and fixed costs of $900,000, SGE needs evidence that the policy reduces incidents before extending it to the whole workforce.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using SGE's survey, costs and skills data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in lithium and solar-component costs will affect SGE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.50%): If SGE's $900,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 1.0% of $900,000 = $9,000 a year (0.01 × $900,000). That is noticeable but small against fixed costs of $900,000, and a $600,000 share issue already reduced the sum borrowed for the $1,500,000 facility. Higher rates may raise the cost of future debt and slow grid investment, but SGE can cap the effect by fixing the loan rate, so this is manageable.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $15.04 an hour): Technicians and site crews are likely hourly paid, so the rise lifts costs while 18 of 75 staff need accreditation. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be honestly invented; the sound comparison is given productivity of 60,000 units ÷ 75 staff = 800 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is bearable; if the skills gap cuts output, unit labour cost rises and the $25.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (13.2% lithium and solar components): The $40.00 variable cost per unit is exposed to these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an explicit bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 13.2%, that would add 13.2% × $40.00 = $5.28 per unit, and over 60,000 units that is $316,800 a year (60,000 × $5.28) — many times the interest effect. Even a $2.00-per-unit increase would cost $120,000 a year. SGE can offset part through tenders supported by 6.7% demand growth and its accreditation advantage.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in lithium and solar-component costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 units, directly erodes the $25.00 contribution that supports the $1,500,000 investment, and is largely outside SGE's short-term control. The interest rise is modest and hedgeable, and the wage rise is serious but depends on unstated hours and on productivity SGE can influence, so both rank below input inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to SGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SGE's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
